title: How the natural mind was shaped, and how the soul came to see
reading:
What the soul has claimed asserts itself with a great clamor, and from this clash a war is set loose within the rational. The proprium does not stay still; it organizes, joins itself together, and by that very joining its claimed states are drawn upward and given the form of a structured world — the natural mind taking shape as if from itself, under permission.

Yet within this forming the Lord's principles already dwell. He does not stand outside what the proprium constructs; he is interior to it, set within the very materials it gathers, so that what is given may in time be refined out from what has been claimed. The vessel is permitted to take shape precisely so that, from within, the discrimination can begin.

Falsity from evil is also at work here, with its own bringing-forth, multiplying perceptions in the wandering. Out of the lowest depth of the natural the figure of the first human is molded — the rational given a body of its own to operate from, the natural mind formed as a standing shape that thinks itself its own.

And then the soul tastes from the perception that has grown in this ground; it eats of the knowledge planted within the formed mind — and its understanding opens. Sight is given. The eyes that had been closed within the molded form look out. From this first opening the whole long work of recognition will proceed: what has been seen must now be sorted, and what is the Lord's must be told from what the soul has taken as its own.

(The chapter is broken in many places; the surviving line of teaching runs from the proprium's self-assertion, through the forming of the natural mind under permission, to the first opening of the soul's sight within that formed vessel.)
